before.content_html:
Radiation All Around Us

Radiation is part of daily life. We are constantly exposed to background radiation from rocks (particularly granite), from cosmic rays from space, from radon gas in the air, from food and drink, and from medical procedures. This background dose varies by location — living in Cornwall exposes you to more radon than living in London, because granite rock releases more of this naturally occurring radioactive gas.

Not all radiation is the same. The key distinction for understanding risk is whether the radiation is ionising or non-ionising. Ionising radiation carries enough energy to knock electrons away from atoms, turning them into ions. This can damage or destroy cells and, if it alters DNA, may trigger cancer. Non-ionising radiation does not have enough energy to ionise atoms, though some forms (such as UV) can still cause harm at high doses.

Key Fact

Ionising radiation: alpha (\(\alpha\)), beta (\(\beta\)) and gamma (\(\gamma\)) from radioactive materials, plus X-rays. Non-ionising: UV, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Ionising radiation is far more dangerous because it can damage DNA directly.

Types of Ionising Radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma differ in penetrating power and ionising ability — and these differences determine both their hazards and their uses:

• Alpha (\(\alpha\)): a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons). Strongly ionising because its large charge and mass interact intensely with matter. Stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. Cannot penetrate skin, so an external alpha source poses little risk to internal organs — but if an alpha-emitting substance is inhaled or swallowed, the radiation delivers its full energy to sensitive tissue close by.
• Beta (\(\beta\)): a fast-moving electron. Moderately ionising. Penetrates paper but stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Can penetrate a short distance into body tissue.
• Gamma (\(\gamma\)): a high-energy electromagnetic wave. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating — passes through the body and is only significantly absorbed by dense lead or thick concrete. This penetrating power makes it useful for both medical imaging and radiotherapy, but means external gamma sources are hazardous from a distance.
• X-rays: also electromagnetic, similar to gamma but produced by electron transitions in machines rather than by nuclear decay. Similar penetrating power to gamma.

How Radiation Harms the Body

Ionising radiation harms cells in two main ways. At high doses, it kills cells directly — this is what causes radiation sickness and burns in severe accidents. At lower doses, it can alter DNA without killing the cell. A mutated cell may then divide uncontrollably, potentially causing cancer. The radiation dose received is the key factor: the higher the dose and the longer the exposure time, the greater the risk. This is why medical imaging doses are kept as low as possible while still providing a useful image.

It is important to distinguish between contamination and irradiation. Contamination means a radioactive substance is on or inside the body, continuing to deliver radiation that cannot be stopped simply by moving away. Irradiation means being exposed to radiation from an external source; once the source is removed the exposure stops and the person does not become radioactive. Contamination is generally considered more dangerous because the exposure is continuous and the substance may be inside the body where even alpha particles can reach sensitive tissue.

Key Fact

Contamination (radioactive material in/on the body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external exposure) because the source continues to deliver radiation internally, even from alpha particles that cannot penetrate skin from outside.

Beneficial Uses of Radiation

The same properties that make radiation hazardous also make it medically and industrially useful. Every use involves a risk–benefit judgement that depends on the specific situation.

X-rays in medical imaging: X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by denser material like bone and metal. A dental X-ray exposes the patient to a fraction of the dose of a chest X-ray, and a chest X-ray delivers a dose roughly equivalent to a few days of background radiation. The benefit — diagnosing broken bones, tooth decay, or tumours — is very likely to outweigh the small additional risk for most patients. Pregnant women and children are treated more cautiously because their cells are dividing rapidly and are more vulnerable.

Radiotherapy: high doses of gamma rays or focused X-rays (or sometimes beta-emitting implants) target cancerous tumours. The beam is directed from several angles so that healthy surrounding tissue receives only a fraction of the dose that the tumour receives. The benefit — destroying a life-threatening cancer — must be weighed against the risk of damage to healthy tissue and the small risk of triggering a secondary cancer years later. For most cancer patients, the benefit substantially outweighs the risk.

Radioactive tracers: a gamma-emitting radioactive substance with a short half-life (such as technetium-99m, which has a half-life of around 6 hours) is introduced into the body. Because gamma rays penetrate the body, their path can be tracked externally, allowing doctors to image organ function. The short half-life means the patient’s dose is minimised — the isotope decays to negligible levels within a day.

Sterilisation: gamma rays kill bacteria on medical equipment and can be used to extend the shelf life of food. The food does not become radioactive — gamma radiation passes through it without leaving any radioactive material behind.

Smoke detectors are a familiar everyday use. They contain a tiny source of alpha radiation (americium-241). Alpha particles ionise air molecules, creating a small electrical current. Smoke particles disrupt this current, triggering the alarm. Because the alpha source is sealed inside the detector and alpha particles cannot penetrate the casing, the risk to the user is negligible — a clear example where the benefit (early warning of fires) substantially outweighs the risk.

Risk–Benefit Reasoning in Practice

Good risk–benefit reasoning requires thinking about the specific context, not just listing generic risks and benefits. For a given scenario, consider:

• Who is exposed? A 70-year-old patient with cancer faces a very different calculus from a healthy 20-year-old having an elective scan.
• What is the dose? Background radiation is always present; a procedure that adds a small fraction to this carries less additional risk than one that significantly increases total exposure.
• What is the alternative? If refusing a scan means a treatable cancer goes undetected, the risk of the scan is almost certainly worth taking.
• What is the uncertainty? At very low doses, cancer risk is hard to measure precisely because the effect is too small to detect against background rates. This uncertainty cuts both ways — it does not mean the risk is zero or that it is large.

Extended-response questions expect you to evaluate a named scenario using this kind of reasoning — not just to list facts about radiation types.

before.content_html:
Two Lessons, Two Disciplines

Climate change appears in two different parts of your course — once in chemistry (about the chemical composition of the atmosphere and the evidence for rising CO₂ from human activities) and once here in physics. The physics angle focuses on how radiation and energy balance explain why CO₂ traps heat. Understanding both together gives you the most complete picture and the tools to answer questions from either discipline.

Earth’s Radiation Balance

The Earth receives energy from the Sun as shortwave radiation — predominantly visible light and some UV. It also loses energy by emitting its own longwave radiation (infrared). For the climate to be stable, the energy arriving must equal the energy leaving. This balance is called the energy balance.

Not all the solar radiation that arrives at Earth’s surface is absorbed. Some is reflected back to space. The fraction of incoming radiation that is reflected is called the albedo. Surfaces with high albedo (ice, snow, clouds) reflect more solar energy and absorb less. Surfaces with low albedo (dark ocean, forests) absorb more. The average albedo of Earth is roughly 0.3, meaning about 30% of incoming solar energy is reflected without heating the planet.

Key Fact

High albedo surfaces (ice, snow, clouds) reflect solar radiation; low albedo surfaces (ocean, forest) absorb it. As Arctic ice melts, it is replaced by darker ocean water — lower albedo means more absorption and more warming. This is a positive feedback loop.

The Greenhouse Effect

Earth’s surface warms because it absorbs solar radiation and re-emits this energy as infrared radiation. The atmosphere contains gases — principally water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane — that absorb this outgoing infrared and re-emit some of it back towards Earth’s surface. These are called greenhouse gases. Without them, Earth’s average surface temperature would be far colder than it is — the greenhouse effect is natural and essential to life.

The problem is not the greenhouse effect itself but its enhancement. As human activities release more CO₂ and methane into the atmosphere, more infrared is absorbed and returned to the surface. The energy balance is disrupted: more energy arrives at the surface than leaves to space, and the planet warms until a new equilibrium is reached at a higher temperature.

A molecule absorbs radiation when the energy of the photon matches a vibrational mode of the molecule. CO₂ and H₂O have molecular structures with vibrational modes (bending and stretching of bonds) that correspond to infrared wavelengths. Nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂), which make up most of the atmosphere, are symmetrical diatomic molecules with no such vibrational modes at infrared wavelengths — they are essentially transparent to outgoing infrared. This is why a small increase in CO₂ concentration has a disproportionately large effect on the greenhouse effect: the main atmospheric gases already let infrared through; adding CO₂ closes the gaps.

Key Fact

Earth’s surface emits infrared. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₂ = methane, water vapour) absorb this infrared and re-emit some back to the surface. More greenhouse gas → more infrared returned → higher equilibrium surface temperature.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Climate

Understanding why the atmosphere behaves differently towards incoming and outgoing radiation requires placing both on the electromagnetic spectrum. Incoming solar radiation peaks in the visible and near-infrared region (short wavelengths). Earth, at its surface temperature, emits radiation that peaks in the mid-infrared region (longer wavelengths). The atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming shortwave radiation but absorbs strongly in specific infrared wavelength bands — precisely where greenhouse gases have their vibrational modes.

UV radiation from the Sun is mostly absorbed by ozone in the stratosphere before reaching the surface. Visible light passes through the atmosphere largely unaffected. The key action is at the infrared end: shortwave in, longwave out, with the greenhouse gases acting as an asymmetric filter.

Climate scientists use computer models to predict how rising greenhouse gas concentrations will affect global temperatures. These models are built on well-established physics (the radiation balance principles covered in this lesson) and tested against historical climate data. Where models from different research groups using different assumptions agree, scientists have greater confidence in the prediction. Where they disagree, this signals genuine uncertainty about feedbacks and timescales.

The key evidence that the current warming is human-caused rather than natural includes: the rate of warming is faster than any natural cycle detected in ice-core records; rising CO₂ concentrations in the atmosphere correlate with industrial activity; the isotopic signature of atmospheric CO₂ shows it comes from burning fossil fuels; and the stratosphere is cooling while the troposphere warms — the pattern expected from greenhouse gas forcing, not from increased solar output. This is an example of how multiple independent lines of evidence converge to support one explanation — a hallmark of strong scientific reasoning.

Consequences and the Need for Action

A disrupted energy balance has physical consequences that flow directly from the physics. Warmer oceans expand (thermal expansion) and melt land ice, raising sea levels. Warmer air holds more water vapour, intensifying rainfall events and droughts. The extra energy in the climate system drives more intense weather. These effects are not uniform globally, but the physics of the energy imbalance means they are unavoidable until the atmosphere returns to a new equilibrium.

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions directly addresses the physical cause: fewer greenhouse gas molecules in the atmosphere means less infrared is absorbed and returned to the surface, allowing the energy balance to stabilise at a lower equilibrium temperature. Switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources reduces the rate at which CO₂ is added to the atmosphere without removing CO₂ already there — hence why scientists also discuss carbon capture technologies that directly reduce atmospheric CO₂ concentrations.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Earth’s energy balance: shortwave solar radiation in, longwave infrared radiation out. Albedo determines how much solar energy is reflected; high-albedo surfaces (ice, snow) reflect more and absorb less.
  • Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₂, water vapour) absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit some back to the surface; more greenhouse gas disrupts the energy balance and raises equilibrium surface temperature.
  • The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming shortwave (visible) radiation but absorbs strongly at infrared wavelengths where greenhouse gases have vibrational modes — this asymmetry is the physical basis of the greenhouse effect.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains that coal burning releases CO₂ by combustion of fossil carbon; links increased atmospheric CO₂ to enhanced infrared absorption and disrupted energy balance; explains that solar panels generate electricity without CO₂ emissions during operation; reasons that lower emission rates slow the rate at which CO₂ accumulates; acknowledges that existing CO₂ remains in the atmosphere for a long time so temperature continues rising until a new equilibrium; notes that energy balance is a physical law — reducing the rate of imbalance slows warming but does not immediately reverse it. lessons.title: Wave Behaviour and the EM Spectrum

before.content_html:
What Is a Wave?

Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium vibrate about their rest positions but do not travel along with the wave — it is the disturbance that moves, not the material. This is why you can feel a sound wave in your chest even though no air travels from the speaker to you; instead, the air molecules pass the vibration along like a row of falling dominoes.

All waves fall into one of two categories. In transverse waves, the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — the wave forms crests and troughs. Examples include light, water surface ripples and all electromagnetic waves. In longitudinal waves, the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Instead of crests and troughs, longitudinal waves have compressions (regions where particles are pressed together) and rarefactions (regions where particles spread apart). Sound is the main longitudinal wave at GCSE.

Key Fact

Transverse waves: vibrations perpendicular to direction of travel — light, water ripples, all EM waves. Longitudinal waves: vibrations parallel to direction of travel — sound. Only longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions.

Wave Properties

All waves share four measurable properties:

• Amplitude — the maximum displacement from rest position, measured in metres. A larger amplitude means more energy. For sound, greater amplitude means a louder sound; for light, it means brighter light.
• Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) — the distance from one crest (or compression) to the next. Measured in metres.
• Frequency (\(f\)) — the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). For sound, higher frequency means higher pitch.
• Period (\(T\)) — the time for one complete wave to pass a point. Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\).

The Wave Speed Equation

The relationship between wave speed, frequency and wavelength is one of the most important equations in physics:

$$v = f \times \lambda$$

Where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz, and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in m. This equation applies to all waves — whether a ripple on a pond or a gamma ray from a radioactive source. You can rearrange it to find frequency (\(f = \frac{v}{\lambda}\)) or wavelength (\(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\)).

Q1: A sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz and travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate its wavelength.

\(\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340}{440} = 0.77 \text{ m}\) (to 2 s.f.)

Q2: A radio wave has a wavelength of 1.5 m. The speed of radio waves in air is approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the frequency.

\(f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^8 \text{ Hz} = 200 \text{ MHz}\)

Reflection, Refraction and Diffraction

Waves can interact with boundaries and obstacles in three important ways:

• Reflection — a wave bounces off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface). Speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged.
• Refraction — a wave changes speed when passing from one medium to another (e.g. light entering glass from air). If it hits the boundary at an angle, it also changes direction. A wave bends towards the normal when it slows down (entering a denser medium). Frequency stays the same; wavelength and speed change.
• Diffraction — a wave spreads out as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle. The spreading is greatest when the gap size is similar to the wavelength. This is why sound diffracts around a doorway (sound wavelengths are comparable to door sizes) but light does not (visible light wavelengths are millions of times shorter than a doorway).

Key Fact

Reflection: speed, frequency and wavelength all unchanged — wave bounces off at the same angle it hit. Refraction: speed and wavelength change; frequency does NOT change. Diffraction: greatest spreading when gap width is similar to wavelength.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that travel at the same speed in a vacuum: approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s (the speed of light). They are arranged on the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength):

Radio waves → microwaves → infrared → visible light → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays

As frequency increases, wavelength decreases (since \(v = f\lambda\) and \(v\) is constant). Higher-frequency (shorter-wavelength) EM radiation generally carries more energy per photon and tends to be more ionising — which is why UV, X-rays and gamma rays are more hazardous to living tissue than radio waves or infrared.

Radio waves: broadcasting (TV, radio), satellite communication. Very low energy; not hazardous in normal use.
Microwaves: mobile phone signals, satellite data, cooking (microwave ovens heat water molecules). May cause tissue heating at high intensities.
Infrared: remote controls, thermal imaging, optical fibre communication, radiant heaters. Causes skin burns at high intensities.
Visible light: human vision, photography, optical fibre communication. Safe at normal intensities.
Ultraviolet (UV): causes skin tanning and can cause skin cancer and eye damage; used in fluorescent lights and sterilising water. Ionising at high frequency end.
X-rays: medical imaging, airport security scanners. Ionising — can damage DNA; doses kept as low as reasonably practicable in medical use.
Gamma rays: radiotherapy (killing cancer cells), sterilisation, medical tracers. Ionising — can cause cancer; penetrating power makes them both useful and hazardous.

before.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces a magnetic field continuously. It always has a north pole and a south pole, and the fundamental rule of magnetism applies: like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Common permanent magnet materials include iron, steel, nickel and cobalt — these are all magnetic materials.

An induced magnet is different — it only becomes magnetic when placed inside another magnet’s field. The induced poles arrange themselves so that unlike poles face the permanent magnet, meaning an induced magnet is always attracted to the magnet that induces it. This explains why an ordinary iron nail is picked up by a permanent magnet even though the nail itself is not a magnet.

Key Fact

Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. An induced magnet is temporary — it only has magnetism while inside another magnet’s field — and always attracts the permanent magnet that induced it.

Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic forces act. Fields are represented by field lines:

• Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
• Where lines are closer together, the field is stronger.
• The field is strongest at the poles and weakens with distance.
• Field lines never cross.

You can map magnetic fields using a plotting compass: place it near the magnet, mark where the needle points, move the compass to the new position, and repeat. Connecting the marks gives smooth field lines. Iron filings also show the pattern visually as they align along field lines. The Earth itself has a magnetic field, produced by convection currents in its liquid outer core — this is why a compass needle points roughly north.

When current flows through a straight wire, it creates a circular magnetic field around the wire. A solenoid is a coil of wire — the fields from each turn combine to produce a strong, uniform field inside the coil with clear north and south poles at each end.

Adding a soft iron core inside the solenoid creates an electromagnet. The iron core becomes an induced magnet and dramatically strengthens the field. Unlike permanent magnets, electromagnets can be switched on and off and their strength adjusted by changing the current, the number of coil turns, or the core material. Uses include scrapyard cranes, electric bells, relays, loudspeakers and MRI scanners.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying conductor is placed inside a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field and zero when it is parallel to the field.

The force can be increased by:

• Increasing the current through the conductor
• Increasing the magnetic flux density (using a stronger magnet)
• Increasing the length of conductor within the field

These relationships are captured in the equation:

$$F = B \times I \times l$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(B\) is magnetic flux density (T), \(I\) is current (A), and \(l\) is the length of the conductor in the field (m).

Key Fact

The motor effect equation: \(F = BIl\). Force is greatest when conductor and field are at right angles. Increasing current, field strength, or conductor length all increase the force.

Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule

Fleming’s left-hand rule tells you the direction of the force. Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger and second finger all at right angles to each other:

• Thumb (thuMb) = Motion / force direction
• First finger (First) = Field direction (north to south)
• Second finger (seCond) = Current direction (conventional, from positive to negative)

If any one of the three quantities reverses (e.g. the current direction reverses, or you flip the magnet so field reverses), the force direction also reverses.

In a simple DC electric motor, a current-carrying coil sits between two permanent magnets. Using Fleming’s left-hand rule, the two sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (because current flows in opposite directions on each side), creating a turning effect (torque) that spins the coil.

Without further modification, the coil would stop after rotating halfway. A split-ring commutator reverses the current direction every half turn, ensuring the forces always produce rotation in the same direction — giving continuous spinning. Motor speed can be increased by using a stronger magnetic field, a larger current, or more coil turns.

Real-World Applications of Electromagnetism

The motor effect is not just a classroom concept — it underpins a vast range of modern technology. Loudspeakers work by sending a varying electrical current through a coil (attached to a paper cone) that sits inside a permanent magnet. As the current changes direction and magnitude, the motor-effect force on the coil changes, pushing the cone in and out and creating sound waves.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scanners used in hospitals contain powerful electromagnets that produce extremely strong, uniform magnetic fields. These align the magnetic properties of hydrogen atoms in the body, and by measuring how those atoms re-emit energy, detailed images of soft tissue can be produced without using ionising radiation. The strength of an MRI magnet is measured in tesla — clinical scanners typically use fields of 1.5 T to 3 T, far stronger than anything achievable with permanent magnets of practical size. This illustrates how electromagnetic principles developed in physics laboratories have direct, life-saving medical applications.

Mastering: Suggests a specific application such as a scrapyard crane (picking up and releasing metal objects) or an MRI scanner (field must be very strong and controllable) and explains why on/off capability is essential — releasing the object requires the field to be removed instantly (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Electric motors are used in many everyday devices, from washing machines to electric vehicles. Evaluate the scientific principles that make the electric motor work and consider how changes in design could improve its performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Identifies that the motor uses a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
Developing: Explains the motor effect using F = BIl — a force acts on the current-carrying sides of the coil (1 mark). Describes the role of the split-ring commutator in maintaining continuous rotation by reversing current every half turn (1 mark).
Secure: Uses Fleming’s left-hand rule to explain why opposite sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions, creating a turning effect (torque) (1 mark). Identifies design changes that increase performance: stronger magnets (increases B), larger current (increases I), more turns on coil (increases total force) (1 mark).
Mastering: Evaluates trade-offs — increasing current also increases heat dissipation in the coil (P = I²R), which may reduce efficiency; discusses how real motors use additional engineering solutions such as multiple coils or superconducting magnets; reaches a reasoned conclusion (2 marks). [6 marks — levels marked]

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Induced magnets are temporary and always attract the magnet that induces them. Electromagnets can be switched on and off and have adjustable strength.
  • The motor effect: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (F = BIl). Force is greatest at right angles to the field.
  • Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the force direction: Thumb = Motion, First finger = Field (N to S), Second finger = Current (+ to -). Electric motors use this effect to produce continuous rotation via a split-ring commutator.
before.exam_tip_html: For questions on Fleming’s left-hand rule, always identify all three quantities (force, field, current) before answering. A common mistake is using the right hand instead of the left — Fleming’s left-hand rule is for the motor effect. For ‘Suggest’ questions about increasing the force on a conductor, link each suggestion directly to the equation \(F = BIl\) — examiners reward causal language, not just lists.
